points: A database keeps data safe across crashes and lets many clients read and change it at once.
A change is written to a log before it touches the data files, and a commit is the moment that log record is safely on disk.
Uber's 2016 comparison found that how a log is shipped decides what replicas can do: physical replication copies disk pages, logical copies row changes.
GitHub shows replication is also how a fleet is upgraded and rolled back, so plan the way back first.

figures.label: active connections: a few hundred where Postgres struggled, about 10,000 handled by MySQL

points: A distributed transaction makes changes across shards or services happen all-or-nothing: every part commits or none does.
Two-phase commit has a coordinator ask every participant to prepare, then commit only if all agree; a saga chains local transactions with compensating undo steps.
Google's Percolator builds cross-shard transactions on a store with only single-row atomicity, using one designated row's atomic write as the commit point.
Cockroach Labs found transaction latency is dominated by synchronous replication rounds in series, and pipelining overlaps those rounds.

figures.label: about 4x overhead over raw Bigtable for a single-cell write and commit
each extra ms of inter-node latency added 6 ms without pipelining, 2 ms with

prerequisiteReasons.consensus: Distributed transactions take from consensus the way each participant's prepared state and the coordinator's decision are made to survive crashes.
prerequisiteReasons.sharding: Distributed transactions take from sharding the fact that one change can touch rows on several shards, which is what needs coordinating.

points: DNS maps human-readable names to addresses through a hierarchy: resolvers walk from the root to top-level domains to authoritative servers.
Caching at every layer, bounded by each record's TTL, keeps it fast at the cost of propagation delay.
Cloudflare found that a design sized for yesterday's load becomes the bottleneck as traffic grows, so it builds each changed record instead of the whole zone.
Slack's DNSSEC rollout showed that an undo is just another change, and it spreads no faster than the longest cache in the path.

figures.label: 150x average speedup of per-record builds over full zone builds

points: Event-driven architecture has each service announce facts about what already happened, and other services react on their own.
The event log becomes the backbone and state can be rebuilt by replaying it, but publishing reliably and processing idempotently get harder.
Zapier found a plain write-then-publish can lose events, so an outbox commits the event with the state change, though a local outbox brings its own scaling pain.
Grab found that cross-AZ traffic, mostly consumers reading a far leader, can be about half the cost of its Kafka platform.

figures.label: over 300 billion events a week the platform was scaled to service
25% drop in cross-AZ traffic after three months of closest-replica fetch

prerequisiteReasons.pub-sub: Event-driven architecture takes from pub-sub the fan-out of one fact to every interested reader, with the producer unaware of who reads it.
